text:
The sound of the hall bell broke in upon the silence and brought her back to the present with a violent jolt. The maid came and said that there was a gentleman asking whether he might be permitted to see Madam. Constance took the card she held out to her.

“Let him come in,” she said breathlessly, fumbling for something in her pocket. During the one minute that passed before Mejer appeared on the threshold, Constance had risen and sat down again several times.

She held out her hand to him.

“It was delightful to see You,” she said nervously. “How are You?”

Mejer stood working at something in his throat that obstructed his words, while he pressed her warm hand with his cold fingers.

“I met Your husband a short while ago; he asked me to come up and see how You were living.”

“Had You not thought of doing so Yourself, then?”

“I did not know—I thought... Are You already settled?”

Constance regained her composure; the pallor had left her face; a delicate red color had come into her cheeks, and her eyes shone with their loveliest brilliance.

“Completely,” she answered. “This is my room. Would You like to see the others?”

He went ahead. “Here is Lorck’s department,” she said when they had passed through the dining room. “Here You shall see: waiting room, reception room, and study.” The last was a small room with a window facing the side street, packed full of books and handsome upholstered oak furniture.

“And here is Your territory?” Mejer asked when they had finished the inspection.

“Yes, this is my room. Is it not cozy?”

“Incredibly so! And with You as its resident.—I do not know whether it is because the room is Yours, or because You are the room’s, that it looks so enchanting.”

She bent down and brushed a speck of dust from her dress.

“Let us try what it is like to sit in it,” she said, pushing a chair toward him.

“Imagine that it is only three days since we arrived,” Mejer began as he sat down.

“Yes, can You comprehend it?” Constance interrupted. “It seems like months to me.”

“Eternities!” He flung out his hand. “Yesterday and today have refused to come to an end; it is because I have not seen You, Constance.”

She shifted slightly in her chair. “It has seemed so long to me as well,” she said.

“I have been walking about fantasizing about coming up here,” he began again, “and then I have longed for You so intensely that in the end I grew accustomed to it and thought it was so good to have something to long for.”

“You speak as though You had been going on like this for years,” she said with a smile.

“And I have incessantly had to think of You as You were on the deck at night—incessantly,” he repeated with emphasis.

“But You must forget that, Mejer.” There was something pleading in her voice. “We are to be friends, only friends; promise me that You will treat me as such.” She raised her eyes and fixed them on him.

Mejer did not answer at once; he sat losing himself in how lovely she was; it was so sweet to hear her voice, to be so near her, and to feel her eyes upon his face.

“You do promise me, do You not?” she added.

“Oh no, spare me! I cannot decide in advance to be this way or that toward You.” His tone was plaintive.

She began to consider his words and stared before her, shaking her head anxiously.

“I have loved You all my life, from the first time I saw You, and I have suffered to a degree of which You have no conception. Give me leave to be as I can and must.” He had risen and was now standing before her. “I will do You no harm”—a melancholy note entered his voice. “You do believe that, do You not?”

She lowered her eyes; her fingers picked at the lace on her overdress.

“You do believe that, do You not?” he repeated more earnestly.

She looked up at him and smiled sorrowfully.

“Yes,” she said, slowly shaking her head. “But Mejer, Mejer, how will this end!” She rose and hurried across the floor.

“End! Why are You thinking of that? Come what may!” he cried passionately. “I am Yours—You possess me; do You hear, Constance? You possess me!”

She held her hands over her ears and shook her head while looking at him with frightened eyes.

“You must not be afraid, Constance”—he spoke more calmly and moved closer to her. “Do I look like a robber or a burglar? I would sooner cut off my right hand than stretch it out to seize You when You had not freely given me permission.”

She began pacing the floor, and Mejer could see that a struggle was taking place within her.

“You shall learn to feel safe with me, Constance—no one in the world can be more tender toward You than I.” He held out his hands to her.

She stopped before him, took both his hands, and pressed them tightly for a moment.

“You must be good, Mejer, only good,” she said in a low voice, looking fearfully into his eyes.

481

Then she released his hands and began once more to walk up and down.

“Constance, I have one request of You: call me Harald when we are alone,” he pleaded. “Oh, do it, Constance.”

She nodded and continued walking.

“Someone is coming.” She went over and opened the door.

“Has Mejer not been here?” Lorck’s voice asked from the entrance hall.

“He is sitting in here,” was the answer. Over her shoulder she sent him a glance that said: Do sit down. He felt electrically touched; after all, it was an acknowledgment of their secret understanding.

“Well, what do you say, Mejer? Is it not quite habitable here?”

Lorck had stepped inside and looked around with satisfaction.

They spoke for a while about the rooms’ excellent location, about the advantage of having the morning sun, and about other such things.

“So we shall move home this evening, then, Constance,” Lorck said when Mejer had left. “You will come down to the hotel with me and pack our things, I suppose?”

“Yes, then let us set off at once,” she answered.

“Oh no, wait a little; it is so cozy here.” He began opening the doors. “It looks positively elegant when all the rooms stand open.” He rubbed his hands contentedly and sat down where he could survey the whole.

482

“And how capable you have been! Come over to me, Constance. Is it not delightful to be at home in our own pretty home?”

“Yes,” she said absently.

He pressed her down onto his knee, took hold of her hands, and began gently rocking her up and down while humming: “Ride, ride, ranke.”

“No, no—stop—I must go out and speak to the maid.” She quickly freed herself.
